chunks: "A power plane is basically a sheet of copper, about half a milliohm per square for one ounce. Every through via that doesn't connect to it still cuts an antipad hole in it.
If you pack too many, the holes get close together or merge, and the copper left between them becomes a narrow neck.
Current has to squeeze through, so you get extra resistance, IR drop, current crowding and local heating. For scale, if 3 amps had to run 10 millimetres along a single 0.
1 millimetre channel between merged rows of antipads, that's 100 squares, about 49 milliohms, so about 150 millivolts of drop, which is a lot on a 1 volt core rail.
Real via fields have many channels in parallel, but the trend is the same.
The plane also gets higher inductance because current has to detour, which hurts transient response, and signals that reference that plane lose their return path.
To avoid it I stagger the vias, shrink antipads and pads as the fab allows, leave solid copper bridges in the current path, and use heavier copper or more planes where the current is large.
Also, vias that do connect to the plane use thermal relief spokes, which limit current, so I use direct connection or many vias for power."
